```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r setup}
library(DesignComplexSurvival)
```

DesignComplexSurvival computes the operating characteristics of two-group
time-to-event trials analyzed with the log-rank test, without patient-level
simulation. This article first describes what the package computes and which
trial settings it covers, and then goes through a design with a single
endpoint. The other articles are listed at the end.

## What the package computes

* The expected numbers of enrolled patients, events and dropouts over
  calendar time.
* The calendar times at which given numbers of events are expected, that is,
  the times of the interim and final analyses.
* The efficacy and futility bounds at each analysis and the probabilities of
  crossing them.
* The power and the type I error; with two endpoints, the power of each, the
  probabilities of rejecting both or at least one hypothesis, and the
  familywise error rate.
* The number of events, sample size, accrual duration or follow-up needed for
  a target power.

The analyses can be driven by the events of progression-free survival (PFS)
or overall survival (OS), take place at calendar times, or mix the two. The
computations use closed forms, numerical integration and multivariate normal
probabilities, so that they are fast and give the same result every time;
they rest on the normal approximation of the log-rank statistics.


PFS is the time to leave the progression-free states 1 and 5, and OS is the
time to enter state 4. Since both come from the same course of each patient,
the dependence between them is part of the model and needs no separate
assumption. A switch (also called treatment switching or crossover) is a move
to the experimental treatment or to another treatment; it can be specified in
either group:

* at progression, with probability `switch_prob`, or after progression, with
  hazard `switch_rate`;
* before progression, with hazard `switch_pre`; PFS is then followed up to
  progression or death, or censored at the switch (`pfs_switch` in
  `ms_scenario()`);
* from a calendar time on, for example after an interim analysis
  (`switch_start` in `ms_scenario()`).

All intensities are piecewise constant, and the number of intervals is not
limited, so that a delayed or diminishing treatment effect is given through
the intervals. Before progression the intensities are functions of the time
since randomization. After progression they are functions of the time since
progression (`clock = "reset"`) or since randomization (`"forward"`). The
death hazard after a switch can be measured on the same clock or from the
switch (`switch_clock = "switch"`), or the switch can have an accelerated
failure time effect (`switch_af`). Dropout is piecewise exponential by group,
the same in all states, and `dropout_pfs` adds a censoring of PFS only.

## What can be specified

| Feature | Options | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Accrual | piecewise uniform, by rates or by proportions and a duration | supported |
| Allocation | any ratio, for example 2:1 | supported |
| Dropout | piecewise exponential by group; a censoring of PFS only | supported |
| Hazards | piecewise constant, with delayed or diminishing effects through the intervals | supported |
| Switching at and after progression | probability at progression, hazard after progression, death hazard after the switch | supported |
| Effect of a switch | death hazard on the post-progression clock or from the switch, or an accelerated failure time effect | supported |
| Switching before progression | PFS followed up or censored at the switch | supported |
| Switching from a calendar time | OS tested alone | partly |
| Timing of the analyses | events of OS or PFS, calendar times, or a mix; final analysis at a given follow-up after the end of accrual | supported |
| Efficacy bounds | alpha spending: O'Brien-Fleming and Pocock types, Hwang-Shih-DeCani, power family, user-defined | supported |
| Futility bounds | fixed (Z or hazard ratio scale) or beta spending; binding or non-binding | supported |
| Two endpoints | PFS and OS by fixed sequence (two procedures) or Bonferroni, with recycling of the level after a rejection | supported |
| Familywise error rate | under the global null hypothesis and under partial null scenarios given by the user | supported |
| Solving for | number of events, sample size, accrual duration or follow-up | supported |
| Approximations | mean of the statistic (two choices) and covariance (three choices) | supported |
| Smooth hazards (Weibull), cure fractions, delays that vary between patients | piecewise constant approximation of the hazard of each group (one endpoint) | approximate |
| Not covered | weighted log-rank tests, restricted mean survival time, stratification, non-inferiority and equivalence, a fixed follow-up for each patient, repeated switches back and forth, dropout that depends on the state, switching started by interim results, more than two groups | not supported |

PFS and OS can be tested together with switching and with group sequential
designs; the exception is switching from a calendar time, which covers the OS
statistic alone. The other articles describe each part in detail.

## Building a design

A design is built in four steps:

1. the scenario: the models of the two groups (`ms_model()`, or
   `ms_fleischer()` for exponential progression-free survival (PFS) and
   overall survival (OS)), the allocation and the accrual (`ms_accrual()`,
   `ms_scenario()`);
2. the timing of the analyses (`ms_looks()`);
3. the test: the endpoints, the spending functions, the futility bounds and
   the approximations of the distribution of the statistics (`ms_test()`);
4. the evaluation: the power and type I error of a given design
   (`ms_power()`), or the number of events, sample size, accrual duration or
   follow-up for a target power (`ms_size()`).

The following example goes through the four steps for a single endpoint with
a delayed treatment effect.

## A delayed treatment effect

The control group has exponential survival with a median of 12 months. In
the treatment group the hazard ratio is 1 for the first 6 months and 0.65
afterwards. Patients are enrolled at 10 per month for 3 months and at 30 per
month afterwards, and the dropout hazard is 0.003 per month in both groups.

```{r delayed-scenario}
lam <- log(2) / 12
ctl <- ms_model(death = lam, dropout = 0.003)
trt <- ms_model(time = c(0, 6), death = c(lam, 0.65 * lam), dropout = 0.003)
acc <- ms_accrual(time = c(0, 3), rate = c(10, 30))
scn <- ms_scenario(ctl, trt, allocation = 1, accrual = acc)
ev <- ms_events(scn, n = 700, calendar_time = c(12, 24, 36))
ev[, c("time", "enrolled", "events_control", "events_treatment", "events")]
```

With 700 patients, `r round(ev$events[3])` events are expected by month 36.

The design has interim analyses at 50 and 75 percent of the events, an
efficacy bound of O'Brien-Fleming type and a non-binding futility bound by
beta spending. `ms_size()` finds the number of events for a power of 90
percent.

```{r delayed-size}
looks <- ms_looks("os", fraction = c(0.5, 0.75, 1))
test <- ms_test(futility = "beta", sf_fut = "HSD", param_fut = -2)
des <- ms_size(scn, looks = looks, test = test, power = 0.9,
               solve_for = "events", n = 700)
des
```

The accrual ends at month `r round(des$accrual_duration, 1)`. The final
analysis needs `r des$events` events and takes place at month
`r round(des$study_duration, 1)`. The type I error is
`r signif(des$type1[["nonbinding"]], 3)` when the futility bounds are
ignored.

The mean of the standardized statistic can be computed directly from the
hazards (the default, following Yung and Liu 2020) or with the approximation
of Schoenfeld (1981), which uses the event-weighted average of the log hazard
ratio.

```{r delayed-mean}
t_fin <- des$study_duration
rbind(direct = lr_moments(scn, 700, t_fin)$z_mean,
      schoenfeld = lr_moments(scn, 700, t_fin, mean = "schoenfeld")$z_mean)
```

## Summaries of a design

`summary()` gives an overview of the design, and `as.data.frame()` the table
of the looks:

```{r delayed-summary}
summary(des)
as.data.frame(des)[, c("time", "events", "z_upper", "hr_upper", "z_lower",
                       "cum_power")]
```

`ms_power()` evaluates a design with a given final number of events, a given
follow-up after the end of accrual, or analyses at calendar times. With the
same looks and test and the final analysis 12 months after the end of
accrual:

```{r delayed-followup}
pw12 <- ms_power(scn, n = 700, looks = looks, test = test, followup = 12)
c(power = pw12$power, final_analysis = pw12$study_duration,
  events = pw12$events)
```

The final analysis then takes place at month
`r round(pw12$study_duration, 1)` with `r round(pw12$events)` expected
events, and the power is `r round(pw12$power, 3)`.

## Further articles

* `vignette("switching")`: the multistate model, switching at, after and
  before progression, the clocks of the post-progression intensities, and
  the censoring of PFS only.
* `vignette("group-sequential")`: the timing of the analyses, the spending
  functions, the futility bounds and the approximations of the covariance of
  the statistics.
* `vignette("two-endpoints")`: PFS and OS tested together with a
  fixed-sequence or Bonferroni procedure, recycling of the level and the
  familywise error rate.
* `vignette("calendar-switching")`: switching that starts at a calendar
  time, for example after an interim analysis.
* `vignette("validation")`: the reproduction of published results and the
  comparison with patient-level simulations.

## References

Schoenfeld D (1981). The asymptotic properties of nonparametric tests for
comparing survival distributions. Biometrika 68:316-319.

Yung G, Liu Y (2020). Sample size and power for the weighted log-rank test
and Kaplan-Meier based tests with allowance for nonproportional hazards.
Biometrics 76:939-950.
